title: Delegitimizing Democracy: "Civic Slackers," the Cultural Turn, and the Possibilities of Politics
text:
# Delegitimizing Democracy: "Civic Slackers," the Cultural Turn, and the Possibilities of Politics

Journal of American History. Published: 2002-12-01. 5 citations.

## Abstract

I swear to the Lord I still can't see Why Democracy means Everybody but me. —Langston Hughes “Poo-pooh! I never vote!” the man sniffed, reclining on pillows, casually puffing a cigar. (See figure 1.) He might look like an upstanding citizen—middle aged, upper-middle-class, maybe even wealthy, wearing a banker's pinstripes, the very picture of masculine respectability—but in the wake of the Great War to “make the world safe for democracy,” postwar labor unrest, race riots, and the Red Scare, this man's civic apathy made him, in the artist's phrase, “The Most Dangerous Man in America.”1 This political cartoon reprimanding the rich for their civic laziness helped publicize a major national effort to boost voter turnout. In 1923 the League of Women Voters (LWV) launched a “Victory Vote Drive” to stir citizens to vote. By 1928 nearly a thousand groups had followed the league's lead with campaigns of their own to “Get Out the Vote” (gotv). At a time when voter turnout had slumped to 49 percent, marking the first time in nearly a century when a majority of eligible voters had failed to turn out at the polls, an impressive array of civic leaders—clubwomen, businessmen, pastors, veterans, and publishers, most of them middle-class or wealthy and white—launched extensive campaigns of advertising and civic education to reverse the trend. The campaigns were massive and included the distribution of 25 million leaflets by the National Association of Manufacturers (nam); door-to-door canvasses and bugling on street corners by the Boy Scouts of America, a project that James E. West, the chief scout executive, described as the group's “biggest national undertaking” since it had sold Liberty bonds; “hundreds” of gotv “community conferences” coordinated by the American Legion in cities from Daytona Beach to San Francisco; full-page gotv ads by the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company in the Saturday Evening Post and other magazines with a circulation totaling 17 million readers; the Voters' Campaign Information Service, a regular Tuesday night radio show inaugurated by the league in 1928 as a “citizenship school on the air” that broadcast to 15 million listeners over the fledgling National Broadcasting Company network; and uncounted seminars, workshops, badges, and billboards.2
